text: What is a typical value? is the first question anyone asks about a column of numbers. A measure of center answers it with a single number, and there are three classic choices: the mean, the median, and the mode. They often agree on tidy data and disagree, sometimes dramatically, on real business data. Knowing which one to report is a core data-science skill.

The mean adds up all values and divides by how many there are — the balance point of the data, using every value. The median sorts the values and takes the middle one, so half the data sits below it and half above. The mode is simply the most frequent value, and it's the only one of the three that works for category data.

Take nine illustrative order values in dollars, with one large enterprise order mixed in: 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 30, and 400. The mean comes out to 61.89, the median to 20.0, and the mode to 15. The mean says a typical order is about 62 dollars, but eight of the nine orders are 30 dollars or less — the single 400-dollar order dragged the mean up to a value that describes almost nobody. The median is much closer to what a typical customer spends.

Because the mean uses the exact size of every value, one extreme value changes it a lot. The median only cares about ordering, so an extreme value counts as just one more value on the high side — we call the median robust. Drop that 400-dollar order and the mean collapses from 61.89 to 19.625, while the median only moves from 20.0 to 19.0. When the mean and median are far apart, your data is skewed or has outliers, and you should look at a chart before trusting either number.

A trimmed mean discards a fixed share of the lowest and highest values before averaging, a compromise between mean and median — scipy's trim_mean with a 0.2 trim on our nine values cuts the 12 and the 400 from each end and averages the rest, giving about 20.71. A weighted average counts some values more than others — numpy's average with weights 3 and 1 on scores 80 and 100 returns 85.0, because the first score counts three times as much.

For nominal data such as region, the mode is the natural summary — on East, West, East, North, West, East, mode returns East. A dataset can have several modes; mode returns all of them. So which should you report? Roughly symmetric data with no wild outliers: the mean. Skewed data or outliers, like incomes or response times: the median, or report both. Categories: the mode. And never report a single center without checking the distribution first.

To recap: the mean is the balance point and is sensitive to extremes; the median is the middle value and is robust; the mode is the most common value. A large gap between mean and median is a warning sign. Next, we measure how spread out data is, because two datasets can share a center and still be completely different.
